newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Content quotas irrelevant to broadcast retransmission -Court.
newsitem.headline: Content quotas irrelevant to broadcast retransmission -Court.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Thursday that member states may not block television broadcast retransmission from other states, even if the programming does not meet European based programming quotas.

Confirming an earlier ruling between the Commission and the United Kingdom (C-222/94), the court found that jurisdiction over television content rests with the member state where a broadcaster is legally established, not where a programme is retransmitted.

The broadcast at issue in this case is the Turner Network Television Cartoon Network. Turner International Sales are established in London, and the Cartoon Network is broadcast over the Astra Satellite under British authorization.

Belgium brought criminal proceedings against Paul Denuit, the managing director of Coditel for infringing domestic Belgian broadcasting legislation when he allowed the Cartoon Network to be broadcast in Belgium.

The Belgian Minister for Communications prohibited the TNT Cartoon network because it consists "essentially of programmes produced outside the European Community and of commercial advertising," according to court documents.
The court found that quota rules under the Television without Frontiers directive have no effect on the issue of establishment and jurisdiction for programme approval.

Noting that the purpose of the TV directive is to abolish all restrictions on the freedom to provide broadcasting services, the court said "it is solely for the member state from which television broadcasts emanate to...ensure compliance with the directive and the receiving state is not authorized to exercise its own control in that regard."
"A member state cannot unilaterally adopt, on its own authority, corrective or protective measures designed to obviate any breach by another member state of rules of Community law."

The court directed member states that relief may be sought under article 170 of the treaty, which allows states to challenge each other for failure to fulfil obligations under directives, or by asking the Commission to pursue the action under article 169.
"Directive 89/552/EEC - Telecommunications- Television broadcasting - Jurisdiction over broadcasters"
Reference by Tribunal de Premiere Instance, Brussels, for a preliminary ruling in the criminal proceedings before that court against

on the interpretation of article 2(1) and (2) of Council directive 89/552/EEC on the coordination of certain provisions laid down by law, regulation or administrative action in member states concerning the pursuit of television broadcasting activities (OJ 1989 L 298, p. 23)

1. Article 2(1) of Council directive 89/552/EEC on the coordination of certain provisions laid down by law, regulation or administrative acction in member states concerning the pursuit of television broadcasting activities is to be interpreted as meaning that a television broadcaster comes under the jurisdiction of the member state in which it is established. The origin of programmes broadcast by the television broadcaster or their conformity with articles 4 and 5 of the dirctive are irrelevant in determining the member state having jurisdiction over such a broadcaster pursuant to article 2(1).

2. Article 2(2) of directive 89/552/EEC is to be interpreted as meaning that a member state may not oppose the retransmission on its territory of broadcasts of a television broadcaster over which another member state has jurisdiction when those broadcasts do not conform with the requirements of article 4 and 5 of the directive.
